Eight million Canadians had had that as a replacement for paycheques lost because of COVID-19. They also moved forward on the wage subsidy and a range of other programs to support workers and small businesses.

The opposition party and the Prime Minister commented about companies laying off workers in the midst of pandemic. Right Hon. Justin Trudeau said that from the beginning of this pandemic, the public servants and policy-makers had been moving creatively and quickly to try to get help to as many people as possible, with the focus being on the people who needed it the most. The Prime Minister also promised that the priority had been to be here for workers in difficulty so that they did not lose their jobs.

Chrystia Freeland (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Intergovernmental Affairs) introduced that Canada had an excellent assurance of its trade with the United States, which was the new NAFTA trade agreement that they had negotiated, thanks to the unprecedented co-operation across this country. Anita Anand (Minister of Public Services and Procurement) explained that Canada was operating in a highly competitive global environment, and the reality was that we needed to make sure we had multiple complementary supply chains operating at the same time, which we had been doing in the past weeks and months, to ensure our front-line health care workers had the supplies they needed to keep Canadians safe.

This was the Children, Young People and Education Committee meeting. It was mainly about the evidence session on the higher education new academic year allocations. David Blaney, who was chief executive of the Higher Education Funding Council for Wales, and Bethan Owen, who is deputy Chief Executive of HEFCW, were both invited to give their views on the financial sustainability of higher education in Wales. They discussed the financial indicators of the universities here in Wales, including the deficit and surpluses, and the impact of the loss of funds were they to leave the European Union. They also discussed the funding of WISERD Education, which was a research collaboration between a number of the Welsh universities, specifically looking at educational issues, and they were providing additional funding to that to add value to the Welsh Government's existing evaluation of the progress of pioneer schools in developing the three-to-15 curriculum in Wales .

The first was the impact of the demographic dip of 18-year-olds, which was deeper and longer in Wales than it was elsewhere in the UK. The second was the increased pension costs and, actually, increased costs generally. The third was the current uncertainty as a result of the Augar review in England, and whether that might play into Wales, and also Brexit.

In all of those instances, there was staff and student engagement as well in the strategic approach on estates.

According to Dr David Blaney, there was always the possibility of structural change within the sector, and that might be one of the solutions that institutions thought about, but it was not a policy position, and it's not always a good short-term response to crisis anyway. But he did not see an institution falling over in the foreseeable future.

The government was content on two fronts: one was that the governance machinery within the institutions was structured appropriately to look at that, but also that if the institutions were wanting to engage in anything other than relatively trivial borrowing, they had to get our consent as well. The machinery was in place and proper governance oversight had been put in place.

The institutional risk review process was fundamentally designed to make sure that institutions were grappling with their problems before they become a crisis. Dr David Blaney suggested that where they had seen things and they thought, 'That just looks ridiculously optimistic', they had just asked the questions. The institutions had been working very hard to try not to take cost out now that they really didn't have to take out, because they didn't want to reduce capacity, which they would struggle to recover again when the financial position improved.

Bethan Owen thought the key bit of that was maintaining the attractiveness of Welsh universities to students, because a large proportion were coming not from just Wales, but from England and internationally.
